title: One number, many moduli: the Chinese Remainder Theorem
summary: RSA and many side-channel attacks lean on a simple fact: if you know a secret modulo coprime pieces, there is exactly one answer modulo their product. We recover that unique x by hand on tiny moduli.

case.name: RSA-CRT fault attacks (Boneh–DeMillo–Lipton lineage)
case.impact: A single faulty RSA-CRT signature can leak the factorization of n; hardware glitching and bit flips turned the CRT speedup into a key-recovery oracle

body:
The Chinese Remainder Theorem (CRT) says: if m₁, m₂, …, mₖ are pairwise coprime positive integers, and you are given residues a₁, …, aₖ, then there is exactly one integer x modulo M = m₁·m₂·…·mₖ that satisfies
  x ≡ aᵢ (mod mᵢ)   for every i.

The constructive proof is the formula auditors actually use. Let Mᵢ = M / mᵢ. Because mᵢ and Mᵢ are coprime, Mᵢ has an inverse yᵢ modulo mᵢ. Then
  x = Σ aᵢ · Mᵢ · yᵢ   (mod M).
Each term aᵢ·Mᵢ·yᵢ is 0 mod every mⱼ for j≠i, and equals aᵢ mod mᵢ, so the sum hits every congruence at once.

Cryptography leans on CRT constantly. RSA private operations often compute mᵈ mod p and mᵈ mod q separately, then recombine with CRT — about four times faster than one exponentiation mod n = pq. That speedup is why CRT appears in almost every serious RSA implementation, and why a fault during one of the two half-exponentiations is catastrophic: classic Bellcore / Boneh–DeMillo–Lipton style arguments show that one correct and one faulty CRT signature can reveal p or q with a gcd. The lesson is not "never use CRT"; it is that the recombination step is a trust boundary. If an attacker can flip a bit in one half, the math hands them the factorization.

You also meet CRT when you combine side-channel residues, when you solve systems of congruences in CTF challenges, and whenever a protocol claims "we only need the answer mod each prime factor." The uniqueness statement is the security-relevant half: there are not many secrets that fit the residues — there is one class mod M.

Worked micro-example: x ≡ 2 (mod 3), x ≡ 3 (mod 5), x ≡ 2 (mod 7). Here M = 105, and the unique solution in 0…104 is x = 23. Check: 23 = 7·3+2, 23 = 4·5+3, 23 = 3·7+2.

When you audit RSA code, look for CRT recombination without verification (re-encrypt and compare to the message, or verify the signature with the public key). When you solve a puzzle that gives you a secret mod several coprime moduli, reach for the sum above instead of guessing.

exercise.statement: Find the unique x in 0 … 384 that satisfies all three congruences below. Answer ZKCTF{x}.
hints: Compute Mᵢ = M/mᵢ for each modulus, then yᵢ = Mᵢ⁻¹ mod mᵢ.
x ≡ Σ aᵢ·Mᵢ·yᵢ (mod 385). Your answer should be a three-digit number.
